case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower plaintiff must prove the employer acted with retaliatory intent to satisfy his prima facie burden under SOX’s burden-shifting framework.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1514A (Sarbanes-Oxley Act whistleblower protection), including § 1514A(b)’s adoption of the AIR21 burden-shifting framework.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Murray argues that § 1514A does not require proof of the employer’s subjective retaliatory intent at the employee’s prima facie stage; instead, the employee need only show protected activity was a contributing factor in the adverse action, after which the employer may avoid liability only by proving by clear and convincing evidence it would have taken the same action absent the protected activity. The Second Circuit’s added ‘retaliatory intent’ element contradicts the statutory text, Congress’s deliberate allocation of risk through the AIR21 framework, and the purpose of encouraging internal reporting of securities-law concerns.
case_analysis.respondent_position: UBS argues that the statutory prohibition on employers ‘discriminat[ing]’ or retaliating ‘because of’ protected whistleblowing implies a motive-based requirement, so the employee must prove retaliatory intent (or intentional discrimination) as part of establishing a violation. UBS maintains the Second Circuit correctly required evidence that the employer acted with an impermissible retaliatory motive, warning that eliminating an intent requirement would effectively impose near-strict liability whenever protected activity precedes an adverse action and would improperly dilute traditional causation principles in employment discrimination law.
key_precedents: In re Winship, 397 U.S. 358 (1970) (Harlan, J., concurring)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that the phrase “discriminate … because of” can be read to suggest retaliatory motive, but § 1514A(b)’s express incorporation of AIR21’s “legal burdens of proof” supplies Congress’s chosen mechanism for proving that causal nexus—“contributing factor” plus the employer’s clear-and-convincing same-action defense—leaving no warrant to add a separate prima facie intent element. Justice Kagan’s observation is decisive for me: the incorporation clause is not surplusage, and reading “because of” to require additional subjective intent would reallocate the statutory burdens by shifting part of the employer’s defense back onto the employee. Justice Thomas’s invocation of Patterson reinforces, rather than undermines, the separation-of-powers point that we should not revise legislatively specified burden allocations under the guise of interpretation. A narrow opinion can simply hold the Second Circuit erred in requiring proof of “retaliatory intent” as an extra element, without prescribing the evidentiary minimum for “contributing factor” in future cases.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument remains that §1514A(a)’s “because of” language carries an implied retaliatory-intent requirement, but that reading ignores Congress’s explicit instruction in §1514A(b)(2)(C) to apply AIR21’s “legal burdens of proof,” which define the prima facie showing in causation terms (“contributing factor”) and reserve the employer’s same-action showing for a clear-and-convincing defense. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, adding an intent element at step one would not be interpretation but revision: it would shift part of the employer’s statutory defense back onto the employee and dilute the incorporated burden scheme Congress chose. Justice Alito’s structural point is decisive for me as a textualist—when Congress specifies both the standard and the burden allocation, courts lack authority to superadd an extra element not found in the enacted framework. Patterson v. New York, invoked by multiple colleagues, reinforces that legislatures may allocate proof burdens; here Congress did so expressly, and we must apply that allocation as written.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that §1514A(a)’s “because of” language can be read to imply retaliatory motive, but that inference cannot survive §1514A(b)(2)(C)’s express incorporation of AIR21’s “legal burdens of proof,” which define the employee’s prima facie showing as “contributing factor” causation and reserve the employer’s intent-independent “same-action” showing to a clear-and-convincing affirmative defense. Chief Justice Roberts is right that layering an additional intent element at step one would not merely interpret “because of,” it would reallocate the burdens Congress specified and effectively collapse part of the statutory defense into the employee’s case. Justice Barrett’s observation is also persuasive under a practical textualism: “contributing factor” is a causation standard that often will be proved circumstantially without direct evidence of animus, and Congress chose that administrable approach for whistleblower statutes. Patterson, as Justice Thomas notes, reinforces that we should not judicially revise legislatively chosen burden allocations, so I would reverse the Second Circuit’s atextual retaliatory-intent requirement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest point remains that §1514A(a)’s “because of” language suggests a retaliatory-intent requirement, but that reading can’t be squared with Congress’s express incorporation of AIR21’s “legal burdens of proof,” which define how the causal nexus is shown (contributing factor) and then tested (clear-and-convincing same-action defense). Justice Kagan’s structural point is decisive for me: adding a prima facie subjective-intent element would effectively shift part of the employer’s statutory defense onto employees and make the defense largely redundant in the very cases where intent evidence is in the employer’s control. Justice Jackson’s practical-consequences framing reinforces that, under SOX’s remedial design, an intent-at-step-one rule would predictably screen out meritorious whistleblower claims and chill internal reporting without textual warrant. Justice Thomas’s invocation of Patterson v. New York further supports my methodological view that we should not reengineer legislatively chosen burden allocations by grafting extra, motive-focused elements onto a calibrated scheme.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that “discriminate … because of” in § 1514A(a) can sound in retaliatory motive, but that reading cannot be severed from § 1514A(b)(2)(C)’s express incorporation of AIR21’s “legal burdens of proof,” which Congress used to implement the causal nexus through a contributing-factor showing and a clear-and-convincing same-action defense. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, superadding a separate prima facie intent element would not simply clarify “because of”; it would reallocate burdens Congress specified and risk collapsing the contributing-factor standard into a motive test. Justice Thomas’s invocation of Patterson v. New York reinforces my methodological bottom line: legislatures may calibrate burdens and defenses, and courts should not judicially rewrite that calibration under the guise of importing motive concepts from other statutes. The better, more workable textual reading is that intent evidence may be relevant to contributing factor in particular cases, but it is not an additional element the employee must prove to trigger the statutory framework.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best textual point is that “discriminate … because of” can connote retaliatory motive, but the statute itself answers how that causal nexus is to be proved by expressly incorporating AIR21’s “legal burdens of proof” in § 1514A(b)(2)(C). As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, superadding a prima facie “retaliatory intent” element would not merely interpret “because of”; it would reallocate Congress’s specified burdens by forcing employees to negate what Congress made the employer’s clear-and-convincing same-action defense. Justice Thomas’s invocation of Patterson reinforces the separation-of-powers principle that legislatures may assign burdens and standards of proof, and courts exceed their role when they rewrite that allocation under the banner of motive-based glosses drawn from other statutes. I therefore remain with petitioner: the enacted cross-reference adopts a contributing-factor framework that leaves no room for an extra intent requirement at step one.

As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, adding a standalone prima facie retaliatory-intent element would reallocate Congress’s specified burdens and effectively collapse the employer’s statutory defense into the employee’s initial case—an atextual revision under an originalist/textualist methodology. As Justice Kagan and Chief Justice Roberts stress, layering a separate prima facie “retaliatory intent” element onto that framework would reallocate Congress’s calibrated burdens by forcing employees to negate what Congress made the employer’s affirmative defense. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Patterson reinforces (rather than weakens) my procedural-fairness concern: burden allocations are legislative choices, and we should not judicially rewrite them under the guise of reading “because of” in isolation. Pragmatically, an intent-at-step-one rule would predictably screen out valid whistleblower claims where motive evidence is uniquely in the employer’s control, undermining SOX’s remedial design without textual warrant.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1514A(b) expressly incorporates AIR21’s burden-shifting framework, under which the employee’s prima facie case requires showing protected activity was a “contributing factor” in the adverse action, and then places on the employer the clear-and-convincing “same action” defense. Reading an additional prima facie requirement of subjective retaliatory intent would rewrite that statutory allocation of burdens and dilute Congress’s chosen “contributing factor” standard, a term of art in whistleblower statutes understood to focus on causal contribution rather than motive. A narrow ruling rejecting the Second Circuit’s added intent element best respects the enacted text and preserves institutional legitimacy by adhering to the established AIR21/SOX framework rather than importing motive requirements from other discrimination regimes. UBS’s policy concerns about overbreadth are addressed by the statute’s demanding employer defense and by courts’ ordinary scrutiny of whether the protected activity actually contributed to the decision, not by adding an extra-textual element.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The statutory text Congress chose controls: SOX incorporates AIR21’s burden-shifting provision, which requires the employee to show only that protected activity “was a contributing factor in the unfavorable personnel action,” 49 U.S.C. § 42121(b)(2)(B)(i), and then places on the employer a “clear and convincing” same-action defense, § 42121(b)(2)(B)(ii). Reading an additional prima facie requirement of subjective retaliatory intent into that first step would rewrite the statute and dilute Congress’s explicit allocation of burdens and standards of proof. Although § 1514A(a) uses “because of,” the incorporated framework specifies how that causal inquiry is to be operationalized—through “contributing factor” causation plus the employer’s affirmative defense—rather than an extra intent element at the employee’s initial showing. Where Congress has fixed burdens and standards of proof in the statute, we are not free to alter them; the Court’s due-process cases on burdens of proof underscore that such allocations are for the legislature, not the judiciary (e.g., Patterson v. New York, 432 U.S. 197 (1977)).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1514A(b)(2)(A) expressly incorporates AIR21’s framework, which requires the employee to show only that protected activity was a “contributing factor” in the adverse action, 49 U.S.C. § 42121(b)(2)(B)(i), and then places on the employer the burden to prove by “clear and convincing evidence” it would have taken the same action absent the protected activity, § 42121(b)(2)(B)(ii). Reading an additional prima facie requirement of subjective retaliatory intent into “contributing factor” is difficult to square with that text and would effectively rewrite Congress’s calibrated allocation of burdens and risk. While § 1514A(a)’s “because of” language denotes causation, the incorporated AIR21 burden-shifting scheme specifies how that causation is to be proven and does not demand proof of motive at the employee’s initial stage. Given the statute’s structure and practical consequences for enforcement, the Second Circuit’s added intent element is not supported by the enacted text.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1514A(b)(2)(C) expressly incorporates AIR21’s framework, under which an employee meets his prima facie burden by showing protected activity was a “contributing factor” in the adverse action, after which the employer alone can avoid liability by proving by clear and convincing evidence it would have taken the same action anyway. Reading an additional prima facie requirement of subjective retaliatory intent is inconsistent with that text and with Congress’s deliberate allocation of risk and proof burdens in 49 U.S.C. § 42121(b), and it would chill internal reporting by employees least able to marshal direct evidence of motive. The phrase “contributing factor” operates as a term of art in whistleblower statutes (originating in the WPA and carried into AIR21) that focuses on causal contribution rather than motive; employer knowledge plus temporal or other evidence of contribution suffices at stage one. Given SOX’s remedial purpose to protect whistleblowers and prevent fraud, courts should not graft a motive element that narrows coverage beyond what Congress wrote in § 1514A.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: SOX expressly adopts AIR21’s burden-shifting framework, requiring the employee to show only that protected activity was a “contributing factor” in the adverse action, 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(b)(2)(C) (incorporating 49 U.S.C. § 42121(b)), and then placing on the employer the burden to prove by “clear and convincing evidence” it would have taken the same action anyway. Reading an additional prima facie element of retaliatory intent into that framework conflicts with Congress’s textual allocation of proof burdens and risks collapsing the “contributing factor” standard into a motive requirement that Congress did not write. The “because of” language in § 1514A(a) identifies the nexus the statute regulates, but § 1514A(b)’s incorporated framework specifies how that nexus is to be proved—through contributing-factor causation rather than subjective animus—an interpretation that is more workable and preserves statutory coherence. Consistent with the Court’s repeated recognition that legislatures may prescribe proof structures and evidentiary burdens, courts should apply the scheme Congress chose rather than add elements not found in the text (see, e.g., Patterson v. New York, 432 U.S. 197 (1977)).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text Congress chose in § 1514A(b)(2)(C) expressly incorporates AIR21’s “legal burdens of proof,” which require the employee to show only that protected activity was a “contributing factor” in the adverse action, while assigning the employer a “clear and convincing evidence” same-action defense in 49 U.S.C. § 42121(b). Adding a prima facie requirement of subjective “retaliatory intent” rewrites that incorporated framework and effectively shifts risk back to the employee in a way the statute does not authorize, contrary to ordinary textualist practice. Whatever work “because of” does in § 1514A(a), Congress specified the operative causation and proof structure for these claims via incorporation, and courts may not superadd a motive element when Congress provided a different allocation of burdens. Where the statute’s incorporated standard is at least clear enough to resolve the prima facie showing, any residual ambiguity about expanding liability should not be resolved by judicial embellishment of elements outside the enacted text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1514A(b)(2)(C) expressly incorporates AIR21’s burden-shifting framework, under which the employee’s prima facie case requires showing only that protected activity was a “contributing factor” in the unfavorable personnel action, 49 U.S.C. § 42121(b)(2)(B)(i), after which the employer can avoid liability only by proving by “clear and convincing evidence” it would have taken the same action anyway, § 42121(b)(2)(B)(ii). Reading an additional prima facie requirement of subjective retaliatory intent (as the Second Circuit did) is difficult to reconcile with that statutory structure and Congress’s deliberate allocation of proof burdens and risk. While § 1514A(a) uses “because of” language, the incorporated “contributing factor” standard is a causal standard that can be satisfied without independent proof of motive at the prima facie stage, with intent typically addressed (if at all) through the employer’s same-action defense and the factfinder’s evaluation of causation. Consistent with judicial restraint and respect for the enacted framework, the Court should not add an extra atextual element that would undercut the workability of AIR21/SOX’s calibrated scheme.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1514A(b)(2) expressly adopts AIR21’s framework in 49 U.S.C. § 42121(b), which requires the employee to show only that protected activity was a “contributing factor” in the unfavorable action, after which the employer avoids liability only by proving by “clear and convincing evidence” it would have taken the same action absent the protected activity. The operative prohibition on “discriminat[ing] … because of” protected activity can be satisfied by the statutory causation showing already specified in the incorporated AIR21 procedures, with the employer’s same-decision defense serving as the backstop against liability where the protected activity played no meaningful role. That construction adheres to the statutory text and preserves methodological consistency by enforcing the cross-referenced burden-shifting framework as written rather than importing extra elements from elsewhere.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1514A(b) expressly incorporates AIR21’s burden-shifting framework, under which an employee’s prima facie case requires showing (1) protected activity, (2) employer knowledge, (3) an unfavorable personnel action, and (4) that the protected activity was a “contributing factor” in the action—not proof of the employer’s subjective retaliatory intent. Reading an additional intent element into the employee’s initial burden would reallocate the statute’s calibrated risk distribution by effectively collapsing the employer’s same-action defense (clear-and-convincing evidence) into the employee’s prima facie case, undermining SOX’s practical purpose of encouraging internal reporting. The statutory structure mirrors other congressionally designed burden allocations that this Court has respected as a matter of procedural fairness, rather than judicially imposing extra elements not found in the text. Practical consequences also matter here: requiring proof of retaliatory intent at the outset would often be an insurmountable hurdle in whistleblower cases where intent evidence is uniquely within the employer’s control.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower plaintiff must prove the employer acted with retaliatory intent to satisfy his burden under SOX’s statutory burden-shifting framework.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1514A (Sarbanes-Oxley Act whistleblower protection), including § 1514A(b)’s incorporation of the AIR21 burden-shifting framework (49 U.S.C. § 42121(b)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Murray argues that § 1514A does not require proof of the employer’s subjective retaliatory intent at the employee’s prima facie stage; instead, Congress adopted a contributing-factor causation standard (borrowed from AIR21) under which the employee must show protected activity was a contributing factor in the adverse action, after which the employer may avoid liability only by proving by clear and convincing evidence it would have taken the same action absent the protected activity. Petitioner (supported by amici including the U.S., Public Citizen, NWC, and Senators Grassley/Wyden) contends the Second Circuit improperly added a motive requirement by reading words like “discriminate” to imply intent, thereby undermining Congress’s chosen allocation of risk and weakening whistleblower protections meant to encourage reporting of securities-law violations.
case_analysis.respondent_position: UBS argues (and the Second Circuit accepted) that because § 1514A prohibits an employer from ‘discriminat[ing]’ against an employee ‘because of’ protected activity, the statute requires the employee to prove retaliatory intent (i.e., a motive to punish whistleblowing) as part of establishing a violation; on this view, merely showing protected activity contributed to the termination is insufficient unless the employee also demonstrates the employer acted with an impermissible retaliatory state of mind. Respondents frame the contributing-factor standard as not eliminating the need to prove discriminatory/retaliatory intent and argue that absent an intent element, ordinary adverse employment decisions could be converted into liability without adequate proof of unlawful motive.
key_precedents: In re Winship, 397 U.S. 358 (1970) (Harlan, J., concurring)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that “discriminate … because of” ordinarily connotes retaliatory intent—has force in isolation, but § 1514A does not leave that phrase to operate at large; § 1514A(b) expressly incorporates AIR21’s stepwise scheme that makes the employee’s showing a “contributing factor” and reserves the employer’s protection to a clear-and-convincing same-decision defense. Justice Kagan is right that adding a freestanding intent element at the prima facie stage would unsettle Congress’s calibrated burden allocation and risk making the affirmative defense redundant or duplicative, which is an interpretive red flag for a minimalist, text-respecting court. Justice Gorsuch’s Abercrombie analogy is also persuasive on narrow grounds: where Congress specifies what each party must “demonstrate,” we should not graft an extra mental-state element absent clear statutory direction. I would keep the holding narrow—no independent prima facie “retaliatory intent” requirement beyond contributing-factor causation—while noting intent may remain relevant evidence in applying the statutory tests.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that “discriminate … because of” inherently requires proof of retaliatory intent—fails when read alongside Congress’s explicit incorporation of AIR21’s burdens in § 1514A(b)(2)(C), which makes “contributing factor” the employee’s required showing and reserves the employer-protective inquiry to a clear-and-convincing same-decision defense. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, importing an additional prima facie intent element would reallocate burdens Congress expressly assigned and risk rendering the heightened affirmative defense largely redundant. Justice Gorsuch’s Abercrombie analogy reinforces the textualist point: where Congress specifies what each party must “demonstrate,” we lack authority to graft on extra mental-state requirements not found in the enacted scheme. Intent evidence may be relevant to whether protected activity contributed to the action, but original public meaning does not support making subjective animus a standalone element that displaces the statute’s calibrated framework.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that “discriminate … because of” can connote retaliatory intent, but here Congress did not stop at that general phrase—it expressly incorporated AIR21’s “contributing factor” prima facie showing and the employer’s “clear and convincing” same-decision defense, which is hard to square with grafting an additional, freestanding animus element at step one. Chief Justice Roberts is right that inserting an intent requirement would effectively rewrite Congress’s calibrated burden allocation and diminish the distinct role the heightened affirmative defense is supposed to play. Justice Gorsuch’s Abercrombie analogy is also persuasive on the narrow textual point: where a statute specifies what each party must “demonstrate,” we should not add extra mental-state requirements absent clear language. Practical consequences reinforce the text rather than override it—an animus prerequisite would predictably devolve into self-serving denials and undercut the remedial scheme while employers remain protected by the clear-and-convincing same-action showing.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument is that § 1514A(a)’s phrasing—“discriminate … because of”—imports a requirement to prove retaliatory animus, but that reading cannot be squared with § 1514A(b)(2)’s express incorporation of AIR21’s calibrated burden-shifting: the employee shows protected activity was a “contributing factor,” and the employer alone bears the clear-and-convincing same-decision defense. Justice Kagan’s point about superfluity is decisive for me: if we force an intent element at step one, we effectively collapse or dilute Congress’s chosen employer-side safeguard and reallocate the risk of uncertainty back onto whistleblowers. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Abercrombie is also persuasive insofar as it cautions against grafting extra mental-state requirements onto a statute that already specifies what each party must “demonstrate.” On pragmatic grounds, adding an intent prerequisite would predictably screen out meritorious claims by vulnerable employees who rarely can access direct state-of-mind evidence, undermining SOX’s remedial design without any textual necessity.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that “discriminate … because of” often connotes a motive/intent inquiry, but that general intuition has to yield to the specific mechanism Congress enacted by incorporating AIR21’s step-by-step burden shifting. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, layering an additional prima facie “retaliatory animus” element on top of the contributing-factor showing would reallocate the risk of uncertainty and make the employer’s clear-and-convincing same-decision defense do far less work than the text assigns it. Justice Gorsuch’s Abercrombie analogy strengthens the methodological point: where Congress specifies what each party must “demonstrate,” we should not graft extra mental-state requirements absent clear language, and here Congress chose a causation-focused term of art (“contributing factor”) at step one. Intent evidence can still be relevant circumstantially, but it is not a freestanding element that displaces the incorporated framework.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Respondent’s best point remains that “discriminate … because of” can, in isolation, sound like it carries an intent/animus component. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Congress did not leave that phrase to float free—it expressly incorporated AIR21’s step-by-step scheme that makes the employee’s burden a “contributing factor” showing and assigns the employer a “clear and convincing” same-action defense; layering in a freestanding intent element would reshuffle those burdens and dilute the work Congress gave the affirmative defense. Justice Kagan’s superfluity concern reinforces the same textual point: an added intent requirement risks making the statutory defense redundant or, at minimum, materially less meaningful than Congress specified. Under a separation-of-powers textualist approach, we apply the burdens Congress enacted rather than import a Title VII-style motive element that the incorporated framework does not require, while leaving intent evidence relevant as proof of causation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that “discriminate … because of” inherently demands proof of retaliatory intent—has intuitive force in ordinary speech, but it cannot be read in isolation from §1514A(b)’s express incorporation of AIR21’s “contributing factor” prima facie standard and the employer’s clear-and-convincing same-decision defense. Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that “discriminate … because of” in §1514A(a) inherently requires proof of retaliatory animus—doesn’t survive the way Congress expressly implemented that prohibition through §1514A(b)(2)’s incorporation of AIR21’s “contributing factor” plus “clear and convincing” same-decision framework. John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1514A(b) expressly incorporates AIR21’s burden-shifting framework, under which an employee satisfies his prima facie burden by showing protected activity was a “contributing factor” in the adverse action, 49 U.S.C. § 42121(b)(2)(B)(iii), and the employer avoids liability only by proving by clear and convincing evidence it would have taken the same action absent the protected activity, § 42121(b)(2)(B)(iv).
